paperTitle: FPTR for deadline-constrained joint beam and resource scheduling
paperThesis: FPTR always retains a publishable feasible incumbent, refines candidates in isolation, and commits only complete, timely, valid, strictly better results.
heroCaption: One bounded run: the feasible incumbent is always releasable, and a candidate takes effect only after the transactional gate.
clockBody: The internal search budget B is 87 ms. The last refinement cutoff is 84 ms, followed by a 3 ms reserve for final validation and serialization. The external end-to-end crediting deadline D is 100 ms.
thirtyBody: Beams, resources, sharing, and finite buffers are coupled. Mutating the live solution can leave a partial result at timeout, so FPTR treats every refinement as a transaction.

heroBody: FPTR targets deadline-constrained wireless scheduling. It always preserves a releasable feasible solution, refines candidates in private state, and commits only candidates that are complete, timely, legal, and strictly better.

paperSnapshotTitle: The problem, mechanism, and result in one view.
paperSnapshotBody: Beams, resources, sharing relations, and finite buffers must be decided jointly. Any late or invalid output has zero utility in the current control period.
snapshotProblemBody: Every control cycle needs a complete joint beam and resource allocation. A late output, or one that violates any constraint, has zero utility in that cycle.
snapshotMethodBody: Candidates are built in isolated state. Only complete, timely, feasible, and strictly better candidates replace the incumbent; all others are discarded.
snapshotResultBody: Across 150 fixed instances, Full improved 3.83% over BeamFirst on average; all 750 Full launches were legal and stayed below 100 ms.
consoleFinal: Emit a legal allocation before 87 ms
problemTitle: Model and constraints for joint beam and resource scheduling
problemBody: Beam choices change available rates, resource memberships shape sharing, and finite buffers change the real value of every move. A local edit can easily invalidate an otherwise legal allocation.
systemModelTitle: Each scheduling run chooses both beam masks and the user set on every resource.
systemModelBody: The paper denotes users, resources, subbands, and beams by U, R, T, and P. Each user has a finite buffer Bᵤ, base link quality γᵤ, and beam capability cᵤ,ₚ. Each resource explicitly belongs to one or two subbands, and a two-member set need not be adjacent.
objectiveLabel: Objective: maximize transmitted traffic clipped by finite buffers
objectiveBody: α denotes subband-beam activation and Gᵣ is the legal user set on resource r. An output has positive utility only if it passes every constraint and is serialized before the external deadline D.
trafficMapTitle: The effective link value passes through a step function before it contributes traffic.
trafficMapBody: This q(z) is a deterministic one-snapshot traffic abstraction, not a continuous physical-layer rate law.
figureProblem: Scheduling snapshot and resource–subband coupling. Figure from the public repository.
problemAsideBody: When refinements mutate the live solution, a timeout or failed validation can leave only a partial result. FPTR isolates candidates, so a failed attempt costs that attempt—not the usable incumbent.
scenarioQuestionTitle: What must the scheduler answer each cycle?
scenarioQuestionBody: Which subband-beam pairs to activate and which users to place on every resource. The result must be completely serialized before the deadline and satisfy every constraint.
objectiveTitle: Utility is actual deliverable traffic, not an unbounded sum of link scores.
constraintTitle: Group six constraint families into three mutually coupled layers.
constraintBody: Radio activation determines available capability, resource sharing determines legal combinations, and the delivery contract applies finite buffers and a hard deadline to the complete output.
mutatingBody: Local edit → constraints not yet repaired → time expires → the current solution cannot be released.
transactionBody: Keep the incumbent → finish and validate a private candidate → commit it as a whole or discard it as a whole.
methodBody: I is the always-releasable incumbent and C is an isolated candidate. Only four passing checks trigger I ← C; any failure leaves I untouched.
commitRuleBody: Finishing candidate construction is not enough: independent validation must also return before the stage cutoff. The four tests exclude partial, expired, illegal, and non-improving candidates.
topSTitle: An exact primitive for fixed-cardinality CG selection
topSBody: When the beam mask, resource, retained capacity, and sharing cardinality s are fixed, the sharing penalty depends only on s. Selecting the s users with the largest marginal gains therefore solves that local query exactly.
invariantBody: If the empty fallback I₀ is feasible and the validator is sound, rejection leaves the incumbent unchanged and acceptance requires V(C)=1. The incumbent is therefore feasible after every gate and before serialization.
tailReserve: reserved for final validation and serialization
budgetRuleBody: Timing starts before input parsing. Entry checks prevent late work from launching, while the post-validation check in the gate prevents an expired candidate from being accepted.
timelineTitle: Bounded, cumulative, and driven by absolute cutoffs
timelineBody: Each stage inherits the best feasible solution from its predecessor and has its own completion cutoff. The tail is reserved for final validation and serialization.
stageBase: Build the first feasible solution with diversified masks
stageGlobal: Reprice globally with buffer-aware marginal gains
stageCg: Enable legal multi-user sharing inside compatibility groups
stageRemask: Repair masks and one-resource allocation from residual demand
stagePair: Two-resource ruin-and-refill to complete the Full stage
reference: BeamFirst is an independent reference method and is not part of the cumulative chain.
methodIntuitionTitle: Separate exploration from the releasable state.
methodIntuitionBody: I can be returned at any time. More aggressive search happens only in C, and the common gate decides whether a candidate may replace I.
incumbentBody: The current best feasible solution, already fully checked and ready to serialize.
candidateBody: A complete candidate built in private state; failure never contaminates I.
gateBody: Checks completeness, timing, legality, and strict improvement together.
commitHeading: Finishing a candidate does not make it committable.
clockClarificationTitle: 84 ms is not the final output time.
clockClarificationBody: Pair refinement cuts off at 84 ms. The 84–87 ms tail is dedicated to final validation and serialization; 87 ms is the internal budget and 100 ms is the external end-to-end deadline.
theoryTitle: The gate guarantees feasibility and monotone improvement—not global optimality.
methodLimitTitle: A guarantee is not an approximation ratio
methodLimitBody: FPTR promises an always-releasable feasible incumbent and accepts only strict improvements. It does not provide a global-optimality or fixed approximation-ratio guarantee.
methodFigureAlt: The complete bounded stage chain and common transactional gate
methodFigure: The complete bounded stage chain and common transactional gate.
evidenceTitle: Quality gains, deadlines, and optimality calibration
evidenceBody: Five research questions examine quality, deadline behavior, compatibility-group stress, matched external baselines, and exact optimality calibration.
rq1Body: Yes. Full averages 3.83% over BeamFirst (95% CI 3.09–4.67%) with W/T/L 127/23/0, and 1.79% over Base.
stageGainCaption: Conditional gains in the fixed order: Global +0.44, CG +0.49, Remask +0.59, and Full · Pair +0.25 percentage points. These are not standalone module effects.
scenarioGainCaption: Full has a positive average gain in all five size and stress regimes. Open the figure for its original size.
rq2Title: Is the quality gain bought by missing the deadline?
rq2Body: No. All 750 Full runs passed independent validation and stayed below 100 ms. Wall-time p50 / p95 is 60.28 / 87.29 ms, with a worst observation of 92.14 ms.
runtimeCaption: Solver wall-time ECDF under the 87 ms internal budget. The 100 ms dashed line is the external crediting deadline.
budgetCaption: Raising the budget from 60 to 87 ms moves average gain from 1.60% to 1.65%, indicating diminishing returns.
rq3Title: Do quality and runtime remain stable as compatibility groups grow?
rq3Body: The CG stress suite changes group size and coverage together. Full remains positive while p95 wall-clock time is reported alongside quality.
cgStressCaption: Compatibility-group size and coverage vary together; labels also report Full p95 wall time.
baselineDetails: Open the full results for six matched external baselines
rq4Title: How does Full compare with matched external search baselines?
rq4Body: Under the common 87 ms internal budget and 100 ms external crediting rule, Full gains 6.58%–8.40% on average over six independent search implementations.
optimalityCaption: The gate guarantees feasibility and strict improvement, not proximity to the global optimum. The wider case exposes that boundary.
protocolDetails: Open the full protocol and counting rules
protocolTitle: Same inputs, objective, and validator - with zero credit for late results.
protocolBody: The single-threaded C++17 scheduler was compiled with g++ 13.3 and -O2, then run on Linux 6.8 with a 2.30 GHz Xeon E5-2686 v4. External wall time covers process launch through output collection. Nonzero exits, illegal outputs, or runs above 100 ms receive zero utility, and an independent Python validator recomputes the objective.
metricBaseBody: 95% CI: 1.42-2.21%; gains are positive in all five regimes.
metricRuntimeBody: The worst observed wall time is 92.14 ms.
metricValidBody: All passed independent validation and none exceeded 100 ms.
baselineTitle: Full led six independent search implementations under the same 87 ms budget and 100 ms crediting rule.
baselineBody: The programs share the input-output contract, objective, and validation procedure, but do not call FPTR core code. The result is bounded to this model, host, and implementation family; it is not a universal ranking of published solvers.
stageGainTitle: Later stages add modest gains without a median-level loss.
stageGainBody: These are conditional increments in a fixed order, not standalone module effects. Raising the budget from 60 to 87 ms moves the average gain only from 1.60% to 1.65%, showing diminishing returns.
exactBody: An independent dynamic program reproduced all 12 audited optima. Full has a 0% median, 3.19% mean, and 25% maximum optimality gap. The transactional gate guarantees feasibility and strict improvement, not near-optimality.
limitsTitle: This is a controlled static-snapshot study, not a hard-real-time deployment proof.
limitsBody: The evaluation uses synthetic static instances, one unpinned host, and a small exact suite. It does not yet cover dynamic queues, fairness, mobility, richer interference, continuous precoding, or deployment traces.
resultACaption: Repository figure over 150 paired instances with five runs each: ordered stage gain, scenario-wise improvement, budget curve, and the 87 ms runtime ECDF.
resultBCaption: Compatibility-group size stress plus 12 small exact cases, used to probe robustness and calibrate gaps to optimum.
evidenceNote: This is a code-only public release. Historical sealed results and the manuscript are not in the repository; performance claims should be checked with regenerated artifacts or separately supplied evidence.

auditTitle: Every reported result maps to a process launch, a generated case, or a checked artifact.
auditBody: A launch is an independent subprocess with its own input stream, execution order, random seed, and wall-clock measurement. Quality uses the median of five runs per instance, averages within each regime, and then weights the five regimes equally. Confidence intervals use 5,000 stratified bootstrap samples.
auditLaunchBody: Fixed case, configuration, random seed, and budget.
auditSerializeBody: The allocation goes to stdout; stage traces stay on stderr.
auditValidateBody: Python reparses the result, checks every constraint, and recomputes traffic.
auditCreditBody: Late, illegal, or failed runs score zero; SHA-256 binds inputs, source, and results.
accountingTitle: All 8,610 internal launches passed independent validation, with zero 100 ms misses.
accountingBody: The four suites answer different questions: the main suite compares cumulative configurations, the budget sweep changes the search cap, CG stress raises size and coverage together, and exact calibration adds independent optimization on tiny cases.
externalAccounting: matched external-baseline launches all produced legal outputs; 219 were recorded as deadline misses by that matched suite.
